claims.text: A stakeholder is any individual or group with an interest in the activities of a business: affected by what the business does, able to affect what it does, or both.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The groups normally treated as stakeholders of a business are its owners or shareholders, its managers, its employees, its customers, its suppliers, the providers of its finance, the government, and the local community in which it operates. A particular business may deal with others, such as a trade union or an industry regulator, and may find that one on the list matters little to it.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A shareholder owns part of a limited company and is therefore one kind of stakeholder, while a stakeholder need not own any part of the business, so the two words are not interchangeable. Ownership carries rights set out in company law, such as voting at a general meeting and receiving the accounts; a stakeholder without ownership has rights where a contract or a law creates them.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An interest is what a stakeholder stands to gain or lose from what the business does, so the strength of an interest depends on how much of that stakeholder's income, custom, amenity or capital rests on the business rather than on how strongly the stakeholder feels about it.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Internal stakeholders are those who form part of the organisation itself: its owners, its managers and its employees.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: External stakeholders are those outside the organisation who are affected by it or can affect it, including its customers, its suppliers, the providers of its finance, the government and the local community.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The boundary between internal and external stakeholders is drawn by membership of the organisation, not by how much is at stake, so an external stakeholder may have more riding on a decision than an internal one.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A person can hold more than one stakeholder position at the same time, such as an employee who also owns shares under a staff scheme, and each position carries its own interest, so the two may pull in opposite directions when a decision is made.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Internal stakeholders are usually closer to a decision and hear of it sooner, so they can respond while it is still being made, whereas external stakeholders more often respond afterwards through the market, through a contract or through the law. That is a difference in speed and route rather than a difference in how much each is affected.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A stakeholder's role is the part it plays in the business's activity: employees supply labour and skill, suppliers deliver inputs, customers buy the output and provide the revenue, providers of finance advance money and carry the risk of not being repaid, government sets the rules the business trades under and collects tax, the local community hosts the operation, and owners put in capital and are paid after everyone else.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A stakeholder's rights are what it is entitled to receive or to do in its dealings with the business. Some are created by law, such as an employee's entitlement to the wage and conditions set out in employment legislation or a shareholder's entitlement to vote at a general meeting; others are created by agreement, such as a supplier's thirty-day payment terms.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A stakeholder's responsibilities are what is expected of it in return for those rights, such as an employee working to the terms of the contract, a supplier delivering to specification and on time, a customer paying for what is supplied, and a shareholder providing capital and accepting that it is at risk.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Rights and responsibilities are two sides of one relationship, because one party's right is usually another party's responsibility: an employee's right to be paid the agreed wage is the employer's responsibility to pay it, and a supplier's right to be paid in thirty days is the buying business's responsibility to settle the invoice.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Which stakeholder rights are legally enforceable depends on the law of the country the business operates in, because employment law, consumer protection and company law differ between jurisdictions, so a right enforceable in a court in one country may be a customary expectation in another.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business decision reaches a stakeholder by changing what that stakeholder receives from the business or gives up to it: pay, hours, job security and conditions for employees; price, quality and availability for customers; order volume, specification and payment terms for suppliers; the return on capital for owners; the risk of not being repaid for the providers of finance; tax revenue and compliance for government; and jobs, traffic, noise, dust or water for the local community.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: How strongly a stakeholder reacts to a decision depends on how large the effect is relative to what that stakeholder has at stake, on whether it has an alternative it can move to, and on how much influence it can bring to bear, which comes from the business's dependence on it, from the law, or from its ability to act together with others.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The reactions open to a stakeholder differ by group: employees can reduce effort, leave, or act collectively through a trade union; customers can buy less or switch supplier; suppliers can tighten credit terms or give priority to other buyers; providers of finance can reprice or restrict further credit; a local community can object through the local authority or the press; and government can regulate, fine or withdraw a licence.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A stakeholder reaction feeds back into the business's own position, because the resources stakeholders supply - labour, inputs, custom, credit and the permission to operate - are the resources the decision depends on, so a decision that saves money directly can cost more than it saves once the reaction is valued.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Each stakeholder group brings its own aims to a business: owners generally want a return on the capital they have put in; employees want pay, security, conditions and promotion; customers want quality and reliability at a price they think fair; suppliers want prompt payment and repeat orders they can plan around; providers of finance want interest and repayment on the dates agreed and the risk of default kept low; government wants tax revenue, employment and compliance with the law; and the local community wants jobs and as little nuisance as the operation can manage. These are tendencies, and an individual stakeholder may want something else.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A stakeholder aim reaches a business decision through the pressure that stakeholder can apply: an owner's vote at a general meeting and power to replace directors, an employee's willingness to work and bargaining through a recognised union, a customer's purchase, a supplier's terms and whether it offers credit at all, a finance provider's conditions on the money, and a government's power to regulate, tax and licence. An aim carrying no pressure changes little.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The weight a stakeholder's aims carry in a decision tends to rise with how much the business depends on that stakeholder and with how easily that stakeholder can act together with others or be replaced, rather than with how reasonable the aim is.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A stakeholder aim enters a decision either as an objective the business adopts, such as a pay settlement it commits to or a service standard it publishes, or as a constraint it works within, such as an emissions limit it must not exceed; a constraint cannot be traded off against profit in the way an objective can.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Accountability means being required to explain and justify decisions to the parties affected by them and to accept the consequences of those decisions. Disclosure with no consequence attached to it is information rather than accountability.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business is held to account through identifiable channels: the annual report, audited financial statements and the general meeting for owners; periodic information for the providers of finance; contracts, published service standards and remedies for breach for customers and suppliers; tax returns, regulatory filings and inspection for government; consultation and recognised bargaining for employees; and public statements, planning consultations and press attention for the local community.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business needs to be accountable partly because company law and regulation require it of some ownership forms, and partly because the parties it depends on commit labour, custom, credit and goods on the strength of what they can find out about it, so where information is withheld those parties tend to protect themselves by asking a higher price, shorter terms or security, or by going elsewhere. Accountability also surfaces disagreement early, while there is still scope to settle it cheaply.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: How much formal accountability a business carries varies with how it is owned: a sole trader answers mainly to the parties it has contracted with and to the tax authority, while a public limited company additionally reports to its shareholders and to the market under company law, on a timetable it does not set.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Conflict between stakeholders follows from the finiteness of a business's money and capacity: N$1 of profit paid out as dividend is not available to pay as wages, to fund a price cut or to reinvest in cleaner equipment, and each of those uses serves a different stakeholder.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The conflicts that recur in practice are owners wanting larger distributions against employees wanting higher pay, customers wanting lower prices against owners wanting wider margins, the local community wanting less nuisance against owners wanting lower costs, managers wanting the business bigger against owners wanting the return now, and suppliers wanting payment in thirty days against a business wanting to hold its cash longer.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A difference in aims is not by itself a conflict: aims conflict where meeting one measurably reduces how far another can be met, and aims are complementary where meeting one helps the other, as when training raises product quality for the customer, earning power for the employee and margin for the owner at the same time.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Conflict tends to be sharpest where the trade-off is immediate and visible while the benefit is diffuse, where the stakeholder bearing the cost cannot be compensated because the business has no contract with it, and where the business is under financial pressure, since meeting two aims at once usually costs more than meeting one.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business's objectives change over time - typically survival first, then profit, then growth, and sometimes the later addition of social or environmental objectives - in response to its circumstances, and a business may move back down that sequence when trading conditions turn.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A change of objective changes stakeholders' positions because it redirects the business's money, capacity and attention. A shift from distributing profit to financing growth gives owners less now in exchange for a larger business later, raises orders for suppliers, gives employees promotion opportunities alongside more change and training, and leaves the providers of finance watching a risk profile that rises where the growth is financed by borrowing.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A shift to a survival objective concentrates the cost on the stakeholders whose payments the business can reduce quickest - usually employees through reduced hours or job losses, and suppliers through delayed payment and smaller orders - because those are the outflows most easily changed in the short run, while owners lose the distribution later than employees lose the hours.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Adding an environmental or social objective typically raises costs before it raises revenue, so owners carry a lower return in the short term while the local community gains sooner; whether owners are compensated depends on whether enough customers pay more for the cleaner product and on whether regulation obliges competitors to meet the same standard.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope for topic 1.5. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
